items.title: How Cloudflare WAF helps protect against Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938)

sentences.en: How Cloudflare WAF helps protect against Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938).

On November 17, 2026, the security research company Calif disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) , a memory-corruption vulnerability in the Base64 decoder of OpenJDK, the most widely used Java runtime.
Under the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) 4.0, it scores 9.2 out of 10 (Critical).
The flaw affects Java.
OpenJDK published a security advisory and Oracle released patched builds in its November 2026 Critical Patch Update the same day, at 21:00 UTC.
The vulnerability lets a remote attacker with no credentials send malformed Base64 data to a Java application and overwrite memory next to the decoded output.
Calif turned that overwrite into a leak of heap memory, similar to Heartbleed , and into remote code execution.

Calif demonstrated pre-authentication remote code execution against Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate in their default configurations, and post-authentication remote code execution against Apache Kafka, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker.
Cloudflare has released a new set of rules in the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset designed to detect malformed Base64 input patterns associated with this vulnerability.

The rules are available on Pro, Business and Enterprise plans and are enabled by default with the Log action because malformed input and some benign application-specific token formats can resemble exploitation attempts.
Blocking by default could therefore disrupt legitimate traffic.
Customers can review matching requests in Security Events now and change the rules action to Block once they confirm it does not affect legitimate traffic.

items.title: Quad9’s withdrawal from France: A canary in the coal mine

sentences.en: Quad9’s withdrawal from France: A canary in the coal mine.
Last month, the Swiss non-profit foundation Quad9 announced that it will withdraw its free public DNS resolver from France.

This difficult decision followed months of litigation and a French court ruling that imposed daily financial penalties on Quad9 for failing to block domains associated with alleged copyright infringement.
Quad9’s departure from France is both disheartening and understandable.

The court’s ruling put the organization in the impossible bind of having to choose between crippling litigation and penalties, or fundamentally altering its service in a way that would undermine the privacy and security of its users.
Left with no good option, Quad9 is choosing the exit door instead.

The withdrawal of a basic infrastructure service from France fundamentally harms the free and open Internet, and it should serve as a warning of the damage that will result if rightsholders and policymakers continue demanding maximal blocking across every layer of the Internet.
It not only deprives French Internet users of a trustworthy and important tool; it creates a real risk of disruption to their daily lives.

Quad9’s resolver is used by a wide variety of individuals and organizations in France — including government bodies, educational institutions, hospitals, and utilities — and Quad9 has no way to directly notify those individuals and institutions that their resolver will soon stop working.
If the affected parties do not change their resolver before Quad9 removes its service, their Internet will fail with no explanation.
Quad9 is not the first public DNS resolver to withdraw from a country following blocking orders, and it almost certainly won’t be the last.
Cisco previously withdrew its OpenDNS resolver from France, Portugal, and Belgium (temporarily) under similar circumstances.

items.title: Maintainers don’t need more AI bug reports. They need fixes.

sentences.en: Maintainers don’t need more AI bug reports.
They need fixes.
AI has made finding potential vulnerabilities fast and cheap.
Fixing them still takes human judgment, and in open source, that work falls to maintainers.
Many are already flooded with AI-generated security findings, including duplicates and reports that aren t vulnerabilities at all.
Another raw scan doesn t help them.
Anyone pointing a new model at a project should ask its maintainers first and come with fixes, not just findings.
Maintainers are under intense pressure from this flood of reports.
As Christian Grobmeier, a maintainer of Log4j, has put it, the AI defending open source has to be better than the AI attacking it .
AI shouldn t add to maintainers workload.
So, with maintainers, GitHub and Microsoft ran a pilot together: could AI help maintainers ship fixes instead of handing them more findings?

GitHub and Microsoft are using Codename MDASH , Microsoft s multi-model agentic scanning harness, to find and fix security vulnerabilities in widely used open source software, strengthening the foundation that much of the world s code is built on.

items.title: Building the Agent Host Protocol for sessions that continue across devices

sentences.en: Building the Agent Host Protocol for sessions that continue across devices.
Models are now good enough to work for hours or even days on their own.
You don t have to watch over every thing they do, but you still need to be able to check in, no matter where you are.
An agent can t live only inside one application.
The work should continue even If you close a window or switch devices.
In GitHub Copilot you can start an agent session in one place and pick it up in another.
This session continuity runs on the Agent Host Protocol (AHP), an open standard built first in VS Code and adopted across GitHub.
Here s how it works, what we learned building it, and how you can use it to bring your agents into your own apps and workflows.
Why one integration per client stopped working GitHub Copilot was first built in VS Code as an extension that bundled its own harness.
This gave you access to your agents in VS Code, but it tied their lifetime to the editor.
Extensions are attached to a single VS Code window.
Close that window, and the agent is gone.

As AWS re:Invent is around the corner, we’re proud to recognize a new group of AWS Heroes .
Every Hero finds their own way to give back, whether through sharing what they know, bringing people together, or building tools that help others succeed.

Andres Moreno – El Paso, United States Serverless Hero Andres Moreno leads the Cloud del Norte AWS User Group and is a former AWS Community Builder.

On his blog, And More Dev, and at conferences and community events, he explains serverless, cloud native architectures, generative AI, and agentic systems in ways that make new technology easier to try.
Andres puts special energy into supporting builders across Latin America and helping them explore what’s possible on AWS.
Geethika Guruge – Auckland, New Zealand Community Hero Geethika Guruge is a Principal Consultant at Mantel Group whose work spans serverless, DevOps, cloud infrastructure, and agentic AI.
Geethika has shared real lessons from building agentic applications and leading large migration and modernization programs at AWS re:Invent, AWS Summits, and AWS Community Days.
At home in Auckland, Geethika organizes local AWS meetups that encourage grassroots innovation and mentors the next generation of cloud architects and leaders.

Jéssica Cristina Coelho – Belo Horizonte, Brazil Data Hero Jéssica Cristina Coelho is a Database Reliability Engineer and a former AWS Community Builder with more than 15 years of experience in databases, cloud, and data engineering.
